bib.title: AgentBoard: An Analytical Evaluation Board of Multi-turn LLM Agents
bib.venue: NeurIPS 2024 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks

question: How can LLM agents be evaluated across diverse multi-turn, partially-observable tasks with a metric finer than final success rate and with analyses that explain where agents fail?
hypothesis: Success rate alone hides incremental progress and cannot separate weak models; a subgoal-based progress rate plus sub-skill, grounding, difficulty and long-range analyses gives a more discriminative and interpretable evaluation.
contributions: A benchmark of 9 tasks and 1013 environments across embodied, game, web and tool scenarios, made multi-round and mostly partially observable
A fine-grained progress rate metric from human-annotated subgoals or state-matching, validated against human raters
An open-source analytical evaluation toolkit with a Wandb panel (grounding accuracy, easy/hard split, long-range, sub-skill, trajectory)
Evaluation of proprietary, open-weight and agent-tuned LLMs

method.summary: Nine text environments (AlfWorld, ScienceWorld, BabyAI, Jericho, PDDL, WebShop, WebArena, Tool-Query, Tool-Operation) are unified under a POMDP-style reflex agent with act-only prompting, one-shot example and a sliding-window memory. Each environment has a progress rate (subgoal fraction or state-match score, max over steps); 20 LLMs are run with greedy decoding and reported with progress rate and success rate plus several analyses.
method.task: multi-turn LLM agent evaluation in text environments

datasets.name: AlfWorld (ALF)
datasets.preprocessing: N-1 subgoals annotated with regular expressions plus env success flag

datasets.name: ScienceWorld (SW)
datasets.preprocessing: subgoals re-annotated as necessary observations; tools and rooms fixed in task text; 36 examples (40%) adapted to a single subgoal set

datasets.name: BabyAI (BA)
datasets.preprocessing: text actions and textual observations; high-level actions added; denser subgoal progress; 4 examples (3%) adapted

datasets.name: Jericho (JC)
datasets.preprocessing: goals rewritten so games finish within 15 subgoals (originals need 50-300 steps)

datasets.name: PDDL (PL)
datasets.source: Vallati et al. 2015; PDDLGym (Silver and Chitnis 2020)
datasets.preprocessing: 4 domains (Gripper, Barman, Blocksworld, Tyreworld), 10-20 problems each curated by authors; parser rules give text observations

datasets.name: WebShop (WS)
datasets.preprocessing: improved error feedback; progress rate = mean of scores on search, product and confirmation pages

datasets.name: WebArena (WA)
datasets.split: filtered from original: Site Navigation and Contact & Config sub-tasks
datasets.preprocessing: stepwise progress rate from URL match (domain, LCS on query, F1 on params) plus content match

datasets.name: Tool-Query (TQ)
datasets.source: authors; Open-Meteo, TMDB, Citation Network Dataset
datasets.preprocessing: questions chosen so SOTA LLMs cannot answer directly; subgoals = outputs of annotated golden actions

datasets.name: Tool-Operation (TO)
datasets.source: authors; Todoist API, Google Sheets API
datasets.preprocessing: Todo uses subgoals; Sheet uses fraction of cells matching golden spreadsheet

other.api: Anthropic claude-2 (2023-06-01), claude-3 haiku (2024-03-07), Google gemini-1.5-flash

other.note: Table 12 lists Llama2-13b as meta-llama/CodeLlama13b-chat-hf (likely typo)
agent-instruction-tuned models; xLAM checkpoint not listed in Table 12

inference.samples: inferred: one run per model in main Table 3; Appendix D gives confidence intervals for GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Mistral-7b, Llama-13b only, number of runs not stated
inference.prompting: act-only reflex agent, unified template of system prompt, instruction, one-shot in-context example, goal, trajectory; sliding window keeps most recent history within model context

parameters.serving: open-weight models via vLLM; proprietary via Azure/Anthropic/Google APIs

other.memory_ablation: Sliding Window vs Cutoff vs Summary on GPT-3.5-Turbo (4k) and Mistral-7b (32k), Table 10

metrics.name: Progress rate
metrics.definition: r_t = max over i<=t of matching score f(s_i,g) (continuous tasks) or of mean over K subgoals of regex-matched f(s_i,g_k) in {0,1}; 0 at start, 1 when task done

metrics.name: Success rate
metrics.definition: proportion of tasks completed within T interactions (progress rate == 1)

metrics.name: Sub-skill score
metrics.definition: per-task difficulty ratings (1-3, spatial navigation 0-1) from Table 11 used to weight a score per skill: memory, planning, world modeling, self-reflection, grounding, spatial navigation; exact aggregation formula not given

baselines: 20 evaluated LLMs compared among themselves; ReAct and Cutoff/Summary memory as framework ablations
eval.protocol: Human validation: 60 trajectories per task for 8 tasks from GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo and DeepSeek-67b; four authors each rate progress on a five-level scale 0% to 100% in 25% steps, mean taken, Pearson correlation and Fleiss kappa reported. Hard/easy split by subgoal count cutoff (Table 14). Annotation checked in three verification rounds.

prompts.text: You are a helpful assistant. Generate your next step of action after Action. Action must not be empty. e.g. Action: put down cup.

evidence.quote: We use greedy decoding strategy and set temperature to zero for better replicacy

results.claim: GPT-4 has the best average progress rate and success rate among 20 evaluated models.
results.setup: AgentBoard 9 tasks, 1013 environments, one-shot act-only agent, greedy decoding
results.quote: GPT-4 significantly surpasses other LLMs, achieving an average progress rate of 70.0%, followed by Claude and Gemini.
results.note: Success rate average 47.9; text says Claude and Gemini follow, but Table 3 puts Claude2 then Gemini1.5-Flash on progress rate and Gemini then Claude3-Haiku next

results.claim: Progress rate separates models whose success rates are both near zero.
results.metric: progress rate vs success rate, Llama2-13b vs Mistral-7b
results.quote: but their progress rates differ significantly: 18.9% for Llama2-13b and 24.6% for Mistral-7b.

results.claim: Automatic progress rate correlates with human judgment of progress above 0.95 on all validated tasks.
results.setup: Trajectories from GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, DeepSeek-67b; raters pick from 0/25/50/75/100%
results.quote: Results show that progress rate highly correlates with human assessment on the progress where the Pearson correlation exceeds 0.95 on all tasks, and substantial agreement is reached among the annotators.
results.note: Fig 3 panel labels show rho 0.95-0.99 and kappa 0.73-0.91; the text says all 8 tasks but the paper has 9 environments (Tool counted once in Fig 3 as Tool)

results.claim: Hard examples cause a large drop for GPT-4: success falls from 85.0 to 24.9 in embodied AI.
results.metric: success rate easy vs hard, Embodied AI
results.setup: Easy/hard split by subgoal count (Table 14 cutoffs); GPT-4
results.quote: Unsurprisingly, all models show a significant performance drop on hard examples
results.table: Table 5, row GPT-4 Success, columns Embodied AI Easy/Hard (85.0, 24.9)

results.claim: Code-trained models do better as agents: CodeLlama-34b beats Llama2-70b by 6.2 progress points.
results.setup: Open-weight chat models, average over 9 tasks
results.quote: CodeLlama-34b outperforms Llama2-70b by 6.2% in terms of progress rate

results.claim: Agent instruction tuning helps: AgentLM-70b improves over its Llama2-70b base by 9.5 progress points and 10.2 success points.
results.setup: AgentLM-70b trained on AlfWorld and WebShop trajectories, evaluated on all 9 tasks
results.quote: AgentLM-70b, trained on Llama2-70b, improves by 9.5% in terms of progress rate and 10.2% in terms

results.claim: xLAM-70b is among the strongest open-weight models with 20.4% average success rate, above GPT-3.5-Turbo.
results.quote: xLAM-70b is one of the strongest open-weight models with a success rate of 20.4% surpassing GPT-3.5-Turbo.

results.claim: Proprietary models show higher grounding accuracy than open-weight ones; GPT-4 averages 85.6%.
results.setup: Share of valid actions across 9 tasks
results.quote: Open-weight models generally have lower grounding accuracy than proprietary ones.

results.claim: Instruction tuning alone raises grounding but not overall agent performance: Vicuna-13b-16k has 68.7% grounding yet weak main results.
results.quote: Vicuna-13b-16k, despite lower main results, achieves a grounding score of 68.7%, comparable to DeepSeek-67b and Claude2.

results.claim: Open-weight models mostly stop progressing after about 6 steps while GPT-4 and Claude2 keep improving on AlfWorld and PDDL.
results.setup: Progress rate vs step up to 30 steps, Fig 4
results.quote: peak early and generally stop progressing after about 6 steps

results.claim: ReAct gives inconsistent gains over Act with GPT-3.5-Turbo, so the benchmark uses Act.
results.setup: GPT-3.5-Turbo; Tool-Operation shown; AlfWorld 35.6/17.2 vs 37.9/8.2, PDDL 25.0/5.0 vs 17.1/3.3, Tool-Query 69.4/45.0 vs 70.0/50.0
results.quote: our experiments on GPT-3.5-Turbo show inconsistent improvement of ReAct over performance of Act
results.note: Authors' explanation (thoughts pressure context in up to 30 interactions) is a hypothesis, not tested

results.claim: Sliding-window memory beats cutoff and summary for a 4k-context model but makes almost no difference for a 32k-context model.
results.setup: GPT-3.5-Turbo (4k) with sliding vs cutoff vs summary; Mistral-7b (32k) 24.6/3.9 vs 24.0/3.8 vs 23.9/4.0
results.quote: First, the memory component design barely affects models with long context length (Mistral), while greatly affects GPT-3.5-Turbo.
results.table: Table 10, rows GPT-3.5 + sliding / cutoff / summary, column Avg.

results.claim: Run-to-run variance is large for proprietary models on some tasks; GPT-4 ALF progress rate is 69.1 +/- 11.6.
results.setup: Appendix D, GPT-4 on AlfWorld; Mistral-7b intervals are far smaller
results.quote: Open-source models demonstrate smaller deviations as we have chosen to use smaller temperatures to ensure the reproducibility of the experiments.
results.note: Table 6 GPT-4 ALF 69.1 differs from Table 3 65.5; Table 6 Avg 70.3 vs Table 3 70.0; number of runs and CI method not stated

results.claim: Most models fail to explore the minimum number of locations needed in partially observable tasks.
results.setup: Table 8 compares explored rooms/containers/places with the minimum required
results.quote: Most models are unable to explore the minimum number of locations necessary to complete the goal.
results.table: Table 8, row Jericho - Zork3, columns Minimum and GPT-4 (11 vs 6)

results.claim: Annotation errors were found in 25% of sampled Jericho environments in the second verification round.
results.setup: Second data-check round, sample of 5-10 items per task
results.note: Other tasks: AlfWorld 10.0%, BabyAI 4.2%, PDDL 5%, rest 0%

limits: Progress rate depends on human-annotated subgoals; LLM annotation is not usable because current models underperform on the tasks (Section 7, Appendix B).
Evaluation is only in simulated, text-only environments; real-world variability of labels and security risks are not covered.
Subgoal sequence is forced to be unique, requiring manual task edits (36 ScienceWorld examples, 40%; 4 BabyAI, 3%; under 5% of all problems claimed).
Single simple agent framework (act-only, one-shot, sliding window); more capable agent scaffolds are not benchmarked.
Number of runs and CI method are not stated; intervals reported only for four models, and Table 6 values differ from Table 3.
Gemini1.5-Flash scores may be depressed by security content screening.
Sub-skill scoring aggregation formula is not given in the text; only the Table 11 difficulty ratings are.
Models are dated 2023 to mid-2024 (GPT-4 Azure 2023-05-15, Claude2, Llama3, Gemini1.5-Flash) and the leaderboard has since dated.
Human validation covered 8 of 9 tasks and used paper authors as raters.

terms.definition: A per-step score in [0,1] giving the highest matching score between visited states and the goal (or the mean over subgoals), reaching 1 on completion.
An agent that picks the next action from the goal and its memory of past observations and actions, with act-only prompting.

lineage.note: Closest agent benchmark; AgentBoard argues it is single-round heavy and stops at context overflow
lineage.quote: AgentBench entails both single and multi-round tasks, with mainly the former differentiating open-sourced models.

lineage.note: Multi-turn tool benchmark built on fully-observable tasks
Act-only prompting adopted; ReAct tested as ablation
Product scoring extended to stage scores
Cited for AgentBoard correlating with reasoning and coding scores while AgentBench correlates with MMLU
Compositionality limits cited for hard-case drop
Agent-tuned open-weight models evaluated (Lemur arXiv id shown)
